title: Ownership in Practice
story: A junior developer spent two days debugging a 'use after free' crash in C++. In XIOM, the borrow checker catches this at compile time. Combined with contracts, you catch both memory bugs AND logic bugs — at different stages of development.
why: Understanding ownership patterns — move, borrow, clone — is the foundation of XIOM's memory safety. Contracts then layer logical safety on top.
analogy: Ownership is the foundation of a house (memory safety). Contracts are the electrical and plumbing code (logic safety). You need both for a livable building.
try_it: Trace every variable's ownership in main: who owns `original` throughout? When is `copy` created? When is `copy` consumed? Why can't we use `copy` after `consume_document(copy)`? Write a comment for each line explaining the ownership status.
tips: Move when you want to transfer ownership (the caller can't use it afterward)
Use `&` when you only need to read — it's the cheapest and safest
Use `&mut` when you need to mutate — but remember only one &mut exists at a time
Clone is explicit — you must call `.clone()`; XIOM never clones implicitly
common_mistakes: Using a variable after it was moved — the borrow checker will reject this at compile time
Trying to take `&mut` while `&` borrows exist — borrows must be released before mutable access
Forgetting that contracts are checked on the CURRENT state — if a move invalidates a precondition, the contract traps
